docs.title: msmu.dt.assign
docs.text:
Assign a column in place and record its values for replay.

Equivalent to mdata[modality].var[column] = values (or .obs), or to mdata[modality].uns["decoy"][column] = values with on="decoy". pandas handles scalar broadcasting, positional arrays, and Series index alignment. Returns the same MuData. Values are stored in full in provenance; the computation that produced them is not recorded.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData to modify.

required column str

Destination column name; an existing column is overwritten.

required values Any

Scalar, positional array, or pandas Series. Series align by index. Values are captured in full for replay.

required modality str

Modality containing the target table.

required on Literal['obs', 'var', 'decoy']

"var", "obs", or "decoy" for the decoy table in .uns["decoy"], which add_filter requires to carry every column a variable filter uses.

'var'

Returns:

Type Description MuData

The same MuData, modified in place.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
mm.dt.assign(mdata, "reviewed", True, modality="protein")
mm.dt.assign(mdata, "n_missing", 0, modality="protein", on="decoy")

docs.title: msmu.dt.concat
docs.text:
Concatenate samples, retaining modalities in first-seen order.

Features and observation annotations use an outer join. Feature metadata and .uns use the first available value, without filling metadata nulls or concatenating lists. Provenance joins both input histories separately. At least two flat, sample-aligned (axis=0) MuData inputs are required.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdatas dict[str, MuData]

Dictionary mapping dataset names to at least two flat, sample-aligned (axis=0) MuData objects. Keys become the dataset observation annotation.

required

Returns:

Type Description MuData

A new MuData containing the union of modalities/features and concatenated samples. Input objects are not modified.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
combined = mm.dt.concat({"batch_a": first, "batch_b": second})

docs.title: msmu.dt.drop
docs.text:
Delete a metadata entry or table column in place, recording its location for replay.

target is uns, obsm, varm, a modality-specific equivalent, or a table path accepted by map. A mapping target deletes its key; a table target deletes a column, so <modality>.decoy removes a decoy-table column while <modality>.uns with key="decoy" removes the whole table. Missing keys raise KeyError. Returns the same MuData; provenance and global modality masks cannot be deleted.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData to modify.

required target str

Metadata mapping or table path.

required key str

Entry or column to delete. Missing keys raise KeyError; _log and global modality masks are protected.

required

Returns:

Type Description MuData

The same MuData, modified in place.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
mdata.uns["temporary_note"] = "reviewed"
mm.dt.drop(mdata, target="uns", key="temporary_note")

docs.title: msmu.dt.map
docs.text:
Map source columns onto a target table in place, returning the same MuData.

Table paths are obs, var, <modality>.obs/var, <modality>.decoy (the decoy table in .uns["decoy"]), or [<modality>.]obsm/varm.<key> (DataFrame objects only). Index arguments name matching columns; None uses the table index without changing it. columns maps source column names to destination column names. Identical source key/value rows are collapsed; conflicting keys raise. Unmatched rows receive missing values. Existing destination columns are overwritten. Matching follows pandas, including matching missing keys. Provenance records these instructions, not the mapped column contents.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData to modify.

required source str

Source table path: obs, var, <modality>.obs, <modality>.var, <modality>.decoy, or [<modality>.]obsm/varm.<key> containing a DataFrame.

required target str

Destination table path using the same syntax.

required columns dict[str, str]

Nonempty mapping from source column names to unique destination column names.

required source_index str | None

Source matching column; None uses its index.

None target_index str | None

Destination matching column; None uses its index.

None

Returns:

Type Description MuData

The same MuData; destination columns are written in place.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
mm.dt.map(mdata, source="obs", target="protein.obs", columns={"condition": "condition"})

docs.title: msmu.dt.replace
docs.text:
Replace column values in place using pandas-style replacement mappings.

columns maps column names to {old: new} rules. Unmatched values (including missing values unless explicitly mapped) remain unchanged. Restricted dtypes such as nullable booleans and categories are converted to object when needed to accommodate new values. Only rules are recorded. Table paths follow map. Returns the same MuData.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData to modify.

required target str

Table path as described by map.

required columns dict[str, dict]

Nonempty mapping from each column name to an {old_value: new_value} dictionary.

required

Returns:

Type Description MuData

The same MuData, modified in place.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
mm.dt.replace(mdata, target="protein.obs", columns={"condition": {"ctrl": "control"}})

docs.title: msmu.pp.adjust_ptm_by_protein
docs.text:
Adjust PTM site intensities by parent protein abundance from a matched global dataset.

This computes differential PTM usage (DPU), as described by Demeulemeester et al. (2024): the site's log intensity minus the log intensity of its parent protein in the same sample, so that a site's change is read relative to whatever its protein did. It is not occupancy/stoichiometry -- that additionally requires the unmodified counterpart peptide, and is a different estimand with far lower coverage.

A site's denominator is found through the accessions it was localized on, translated into a global protein group via the global dataset's .uns['protein_map']. Nothing is looked up by peptide, so a PTM peptide the global run never observed is still adjustable whenever its protein was quantified there. Sites whose accessions span two or more quantified global groups have no valid denominator and are left unadjusted; .var['adjustment_status'] records why for every site.

The adjusted values replace the quantification that was read -- .X, or .layers[layer] when given -- the same contract as log2_transform, normalise and correct_batch_effect. A site that could not be adjusted is set to NaN rather than left holding its raw abundance, so residuals and raw abundances never share a matrix. To keep the unadjusted values, copy them into a layer first::

mdata[modality].layers["unadjusted"] = mdata[modality].X.copy()

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData object holding the PTM data.

required global_mdata MuData | str | PathLike[str]

Matched global protein data as a MuData object or an .h5mu file path.

required modality str

PTM modality to adjust (e.g., phospho_site, {ptm}_site).

'phospho_site' layer str | None

Layer to adjust. If None, the default layer (.X) will be used.

None method PTMAdjustmentMethod

Estimator to use. 'ratio' subtracts the protein level, assuming the slope-one relationship mass action predicts; 'ridge' instead fits a slope per site. Default is 'ratio', which needs no fitting and so stays usable at proteomics sample counts.

'ratio' rescale bool

If True, shift the adjusted values by the PTM data's overall median so they read on a comparable scale. A single constant, so it cancels in any contrast. Default is True.

True ridge_alpha float | None

Ridge penalty, used only when method='ridge'. A single-predictor ridge keeps Sxx / (Sxx + alpha) of the least-squares slope, so a large alpha silently turns the residual into a plain mean-centering. Defaults to DEFAULT_RIDGE_ALPHA.

None

Returns:

Type Description MuData

MuData object with the adjusted quantification and per-site adjustment annotations.

References

Demeulemeester, N. et al. msqrob2PTM: differential abundance and differential usage analysis of MS-based proteomics data at the posttranslational modification and peptidoform level. Molecular & Cellular Proteomics 23, 100708 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcpro.2023.100708.

docs.title: msmu.pp.apply_sdrf_to_obs
docs.text:
Project columns of the attached SDRF (.uns["sdrf"]) onto each modality's .obs.

The SDRF spans both axes, so it is reduced to the .obs axis by the match key on and only columns that are a function of that key (one value per key group) are projected. Columns that vary within a key (e.g., comment[fraction identifier] under a channel key) cannot be represented on the .obs axis; they are left untouched in .uns["sdrf"] and skipped with a DEBUG message -- or, if named explicitly in columns, raise. .obs never silently collapses SDRF data.

By default the observations are also reordered to follow the SDRF rows, so an order written into the SDRF (plate wells, acquisition sequence) carries into .obs and into the category order every plot derives from it. Readers order .obs by file name or quant-table column.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData with an SDRF attached via attach_sdrf.

required on str | Sequence[str] | None

SDRF column (or list of columns) matched against .obs.index. Default None auto-picks: after split_tmt (which records its set_key in .uns) it builds the composite [comment[label], set_key] matching the channel_set .obs automatically; otherwise comment[label] for TMT and comment[data file] elsewhere. Pass a str or list to override (a list forces a "_"-joined composite key).

None columns str | Sequence[str] | None

SDRF column(s) to project. Default None projects every projectable column; naming a non-projectable column raises instead of skipping it.

None set_index str | None

After projection, replace .obs.index with this SDRF column's values. Must be projectable and unique across .obs. Default None keeps the index.

None order_obs bool

Reorder every modality's .obs, and the global .obs, to the SDRF row order: each observation takes the position of the first SDRF row carrying its match key, and observations absent from the SDRF follow the matched ones in their current order (none is dropped; removing samples stays with apply_filter). Default True; False keeps the reader's order.

True

Returns:

Type Description MuData

A copy of mdata with projected SDRF columns merged into each modality's .obs and, by

MuData

default, .obs in SDRF row order; .uns["sdrf"] is left unchanged as the source of truth.

docs.title: msmu.pp.attach_sdrf
docs.text:
Attach an SDRF table to mdata.uns["sdrf"] as the immutable source of truth.

The SDRF is stored whole because its rows span both axes -- comment[label] maps to the .obs axis (channels) and comment[data file] to the .var axis (runs/fractions) -- so it is not reducible to .obs alone. .uns is copied through split_tmt and collapse_obs, making it the durable home for the original table; .obs is left untouched here. Use apply_sdrf_to_obs to project selected columns onto .obs.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData to annotate.

required sdrf DataFrame | str | PathLike[str]

An SDRF as a pandas DataFrame, or a path/URL read via read_sdrf.

required validate bool

Validate the SDRF with sdrf-pipelines (if installed). Default True.

True skip_ontology bool

Skip ontology term checks during validation. Default True.

True

Returns:

Type Description MuData

A copy of mdata with the SDRF DataFrame stored at .uns["sdrf"].

docs.title: msmu.pp.calculate_missingness
docs.text:
Count missing values per feature and record the counts in .var (and on the decoys).

Writes .var["n_missing"], the number of samples without a value for the feature, and .var["missing_ratio"], that count divided by the number of samples. With group_obs, an .obs column of the modality, .var["missing_ratio_<level>"] is added for every level present, so a filter can be set within one group. Existing columns are overwritten: recompute after removing samples, because apply_filter does not update them.

Decoys have identifications but no quantification, so a missingness filter has nothing to judge them on. They receive the same columns with 0 / 0.0, which the usual "missing at most" filters (le/lt) keep; a filter in the other direction (ge/gt on missingness) would drop every decoy.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData with the modality to annotate; a copy is returned.

required modality str

Modality whose .X is counted along the sample axis.

required group_obs str | None

Optional .obs column of the modality. One missing_ratio_<level> column is written per level present; samples with a missing label contribute only to the overall columns, with a warning.

None

Returns:

Type Description MuData

A copy of mdata with the columns added to .var and to .uns["decoy"] when present.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
mdata = mm.pp.calculate_missingness(mdata, modality="protein", group_obs="condition")
mdata = mm.pp.add_filter(mdata, modality="protein", column="missing_ratio", keep="lt", value=0.5)
mdata = mm.pp.apply_filter(mdata, modality="protein")

docs.title: msmu.pp.collapse_obs
docs.text:
Collapse .obs rows by sample_key, aggregating duplicates into one row per group.

Common use cases (with recommended agg_method):

  • LFQ fractions (sample × LC fraction → sample): agg_method="sum". Standard LFQ rollup since each fraction holds a different portion of the sample's peptides.
  • Technical replicates (sample × injection/process repeats → sample): agg_method="median" or "mean". Replicates measure the same analyte, so the central tendency is the right estimate ("sum" would inflate).
  • Other .obs axis duplicates (plate replicates, etc.): pick agg_method that matches the meaning of the duplication.

The effect on a given modality depends on its .var structure:

  • When .var rows are file-specific (e.g., DIA-NN psm where the .var index is filename.Precursor.Id), each (sample, var) cell still holds at most one non-NaN value, so this function only reduces the .obs dimension; the actual cross-fraction precursor aggregation happens later in to_peptide.
  • When .var rows are identity-based (e.g., DDA-LFQ peptide modality where the .var index is the peptide identity), a single (sample, var) cell may collect values from multiple .obs rows, and agg_method performs the real rollup.
Workflow contexts
  • DIA-NN fractionated: read → psm/precursor → collapse_obs → to_peptide → to_protein.
  • DDA-LFQ fractionated: read → psm + peptide → collapse_obs (peptide gets real sum) → to_protein.
  • Any workflow with technical replicates: collapse_obs(agg_method="median") early in the pipeline (typically before normalization).

Applied uniformly across all modalities so the .obs axis stays consistent.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData whose .obs rows contain duplicates to be collapsed.

required sample_key str

Column in .obs identifying the group each row belongs to.

required agg_method Literal['sum', 'max', 'median', 'mean']

Aggregation across rows of the same group for each (group, feature) pair. One of "sum", "max", "median", "mean". NaN values are skipped; an all-NaN group yields NaN (not 0) for "sum" as well.

'sum' layer str | None

Layer to aggregate. If None, .X is used.

None log_transformed bool

Whether the input quantification is in log2-space. Defaults to False because collapse_obs is typically called before log2_transform (read → collapse → log2 → normalise → ...). When log_transformed=True is combined with agg_method="sum", the function internally converts back to linear space, sums, and re-applies log2 (i.e., log2(sum(2^x))) — the correct LFQ rollup for log2 input. Other agg_method choices (max, median, mean) operate directly in the given space; mean on log2 data corresponds to the geometric mean of linear intensities.

False

Returns:

Type Description MuData

New MuData with collapsed .obs. Columns in .obs uniform within a group retain

MuData

their scalar value; non-uniform columns become lists preserving the original

MuData

row order, so per-row metadata (e.g., filenames) is not lost.

Notes
  • .obsm/.obsp are not propagated through the collapse.
  • .var and modality .uns are preserved.

docs.title: msmu.pp.correct_batch_effect
docs.text:
Batch correction methods for MuData object. GIS-based normalization, median centering, ComBat, and continuous batch correction (with lowess) are supported. ComBat uses inmoose (Colange et al., 2025), specifically its pycombat_norm function.

For 'gis', 'median_center', and 'continuous' the per-feature abundance scale is restored after correction (gis: the geometric mean of the per-batch GIS levels, i.e., classic IRS from Plubell et al. (2017); median_center/continuous: the per-feature overall median). Restoration is decided for the modality as a whole: when the matrix has cross-batch structure (at least one feature observed in >=2 batches, as at the peptide/protein level) every observed feature is restored -- a single-batch feature to its own level, so it stays on the same abundance scale as the rest. When the matrix is fully block-diagonal (no feature spans >=2 batches, e.g., a per-plex-split PSM matrix) nothing is restored and the output stays reference-relative, ready to roll up. ComBat scales itself.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData object to batch correct.

required method Literal['gis', 'median_center', 'combat', 'continuous']

Batch correction method to use. Options are 'gis', 'median_center', 'combat', 'continuous'.

required category str

Category in .obs to use for batch correction.

required modality str

Modality to batch correct.

required layer str | None

Layer to batch correct. If None, the default layer (.X) will be used.

None gis_samples list[str] | None

List of GIS samples.

None drop_gis bool

If True, GIS samples will be dropped after correction. Default is True.

True log_transformed bool

If True, data is assumed to be log-transformed. Default is True.

True

Returns:

Type Description MuData

Batch corrected MuData object.

References

Colange, M., Appé, G., Meunier, L., Weill, S., Johnson, W. E., Nordor, A., and Behdenna, A. Bridging the gap between R and Python in bulk transcriptomic data analysis with InMoose. Scientific Reports 15, 18104 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-03376-y.

Plubell, D. L. et al. Extended multiplexing of Tandem Mass Tags (TMT) labeling reveals age and high fat diet specific proteome changes in mouse epididymal adipose tissue. Molecular & Cellular Proteomics 16, 873–890 (2017). https://doi.org/10.1074/mcp.M116.065524.

docs.title: msmu.pp.normalise
docs.text:
Normalize data in MuData object.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData object to normalize.

required method NormalisationMethod

Normalization method to use. Options are 'median', 'median_center', 'quantile', 'total_sum', 'pairwise_median'.

required modality str

Modality to normalize.

required layer str | None

Layer to normalize. If None, the default layer (.X) will be used.

None group_obs str | None

Column name in adata.obs defining sample groups. If provided, normalization is performed independently within each group. Missing group values are rejected. If None, no .obs grouping is applied.

None group_var str | None

Column name in adata.var defining feature groups (e.g., "filename" for fractionated TMT or label-free workflows). If provided, normalization is performed independently within each group. If None, no .var grouping is applied.

None batch_key str | None

Deprecated alias for group_obs.

None fraction_key str | None

Deprecated alias for group_var.

None fraction bool

Deprecated. If True, equivalent to group_var="filename".

False

Returns:

Type Description MuData

Normalized copy of the MuData object; the selected .X or layer is updated in the copy.

Notes

When both group_obs and group_var are provided, normalization is performed independently within each (observation group × feature group) block.

method="pairwise_median" aligns samples on the features they share: for every pair of samples it takes the median log2 difference over their co-observed features, and each sample's shift is the mean of its pairwise medians over all samples (the equal-weight least-squares solution, shifts summing to zero). It assumes that most of the features shared between two samples are unchanged. Per-sample medians of observed values are no longer aligned afterward; this is intended, as those differences reflect which features each sample observed rather than loading. A true global change between conditions is removed, as with median. Two samples of a block that observe no feature in common raise a ValueError naming them (for example PSMs or precursors across runs or TMT plexes): normalize within group_obs, or after summarizing to a level where the samples share features.

Every call records what was done to each sample of each block in adata.uns["normalisation"]: a summary table (sample, obs_group, var_group, method, layer, n_observed_features, shift_log2, location_before, location_after) and, per block, the per-sample vectors plus, for pairwise_median, the pair_median_log2 and pair_shared_count matrices the shifts were derived from. Records for the same layer are replaced on a repeated call.

docs.title: msmu.pp.normalize

All parameters, return values, grouping rules, and deprecated arguments are identical; see the linked API for the full contract. Returns a normalized copy.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
mdata = mm.pp.normalize(mdata, method="median", modality="protein")

docs.title: msmu.pp.split_tmt
docs.text:
Split TMT channels in a MuData object into separate modalities based on a mapping.

Splitting relabels the C reporter channels into C x n_set distinct channel_set samples so that each biological sample is unambiguous. Because a given PSM is measured in only one set, the resulting PSM matrix is block-diagonal: every feature carries values in just its set's channels and is missing (NaN) in every other set's. A dense store would be O(n_set^2) -- both the feature count and the sample count scale with the number of sets, which is what makes many-plex studies exhaust memory -- so only the block diagonal (O(n_set)) is stored, as a scipy sparse .X. Every .obs label and stored value is identical to a fully materialised split; only the structurally-absent cross-set cells are left out.

Note: because those cells are not stored, mdata.mod["psm"].to_df() returns 0 (scipy sparse convention) rather than NaN for them. Inspect the matrix with :func:msmu._core._blockdiag.dense_block, which restores absent cells as NaN.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

The MuData object containing TMT data.

required map dict[str, str] | Series | DataFrame | None

A mapping of filenames to set names. If a DataFrame is provided, it should have two columns: the first for filenames and the second for set names. If None (the default), the map is derived from the attached SDRF (comment[data file] -> set_key, one set per file), which requires attach_sdrf first.

None set_key str

SDRF column naming each file's set/plex when deriving the map (map=None). Default comment[sample preparation batch]; name another per-file-constant column (e.g., a factor value[...]) when the SDRF encodes the set elsewhere.

'comment[sample preparation batch]'

Returns:

Type Description MuData

The MuData object with TMT channels split into channel_set samples.

Purity threshold for TMT data quantification aggregation (does not filter out features). If None, no filtering is applied. Defaults to 0.7.

0.7 top_n int | None

MuData object containing Peptide-level data.

"median_polish" applies Tukey's median polish per protein group and "directlfq" applies the DirectLFQ rollup per protein group; both assume the quantification is in log2 space (apply log2_transform first).

'median' top_n int | None

Number of top peptides to consider for summarization. If None, all peptides are used. Defaults to None.

None rank_method Literal['median_intensity', 'total_intensity', 'max_intensity', 'mean_intensity']

Method to rank features when selecting top_n. Defaults to "median_intensity".

Whether to calculate q-values. Defaults to True.

docs.title: msmu.pp.to_ptm
docs.text:
Summarize peptide-level data to PTM-level data.

Sites are localized from the peptide's own proteins accessions and the attached FASTA, so this step does not need an inferred protein_group and the resulting site ids do not depend on any other dataset.

A site's position counts residues only -- the text inside a modification tag is never counted -- so the same peptidoform yields the same site in every notation. Each peptidoform is parsed and checked against its stripped_peptide; a notation msmu cannot read raises rather than produce misplaced sites.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData object containing peptide-level data.

required modi_name str

Name of the PTM to summarize (e.g., "phospho"). Will be used in the output modality name (e.g., phospho_site).

required modification str | Sequence[str]

The modification tag, exactly as it appears in peptide (brackets and case included), or several of them to summarize into one modality. A tag may be qualified by its residue to match that residue only. Examples: "[+79.9663]" (Sage; the decimals follow the search settings), "(UniMod:21)" (DIA-NN), "(Phospho (STY))" (MaxQuant), ["S[167]", "T[181]", "Y[243]"] (FragPipe, which writes the modified residue's total mass). If nothing matches, the error lists the tags the data contains.

required layer str | None

Layer to use for quantification aggregation. If None, the default layer (.X) will be used. Defaults to None.

None agg_method Literal['median', 'mean', 'sum', 'median_polish', 'directlfq']

Aggregation method to use. One of "median", "mean", "sum", "median_polish", or "directlfq". Defaults to "median_polish", which models a per-peptidoform effect and so is not perturbed when the set of peptidoforms supporting a site changes between samples; for a site backed by a single peptidoform it is identical to "median". A sample whose peptidoforms are all observed in that sample alone cannot be compared with the others and is left NaN. "median_polish" applies Tukey's median polish per group and "directlfq" applies the DirectLFQ rollup per group; both assume the quantification is in log2 space (apply log2_transform first).

'median_polish' top_n int | None

Number of top features to consider for summarization. If None, all features are used. Defaults to None.

None rank_method Literal['median_intensity', 'total_intensity', 'max_intensity', 'mean_intensity']

Method to rank features when selecting top_n. Defaults to "median_intensity".

'median_intensity' multisite Multisite

What a peptidoform carrying the target modification on several residues quantifies. "combination" (default) gives it to the set of sites it carries, as one feature ("P1|S5_S8"): a multiply modified peptide's change cannot be attributed to one of its sites, the way a shared peptide's cannot be attributed to one protein, so it is reported as the group it belongs to. Every peptidoform then feeds exactly one feature, and the features with .var["count_site"] == 1 are the site table built from singly modified peptidoforms alone. "pool" gives its whole value to each of its sites instead -- copied, not divided -- so a site pools singly and multiply modified peptidoforms and one measurement can reach several sites. Peptidoforms differing only in other modifications or missed cleavages share a feature either way.

'combination'

Returns:

Name Type Description MuData MuData

MuData object containing PTM-level data.

Notes

Adds <modi_name>_site to the supplied MuData in place. Use a copy to preserve the original. Requires peptide data and FASTA-derived protein_info; see to_peptide and attach_fasta.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
# mdata already contains peptide quantification and attached FASTA annotations.
mdata = mm.pp.to_ptm(mdata, modi_name="phospho", modification="(unimod:21)")

docs.title: msmu.pv.get_log
docs.text:
Return detached, decoded provenance in lineage order, then execution-start order.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData containing recorded history in .uns["_log"].

required

Type Description dict

Notes

Changing this returned dictionary does not change the original log. Events contain parameters, inputs/outputs, timing, parent IDs, and environment references. See replay and to_env.

import msmu as mm
history = mm.pv.get_log(mdata)

docs.title: msmu.pv.log

Log one public call. Nested msmu calls are represented by their outer call.

Parameters:

Function to decorate. Omit when using @mm.pv.log(capture=(... ,)).

None capture tuple[str, ...]

Tuple of parameter names whose values are stored in full rather than summarized, for example ("values",).

() file_inputs tuple[str, ...]

Parameter names whose local string values are input paths, including strings in nested containers. URLs, path objects and DataFrames are detected directly.

()

A wrapped function, or a decorator when func is omitted. Successful calls attach history to participating MuData objects.

docs.title: msmu.pv.replay
docs.text:
Rerun a file-backed workflow, returning a new MuData with fresh history.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default history MuData | dict

MuData containing the original log, or the decoded result of get_log().

required sources dict | None

Optional mapping from recorded paths/URLs to replacement paths/URLs.

None verify bool

Require recorded hashes and verify inputs/outputs (default True). False reruns without hash verification; known unrecorded edits still fail.

True

Branches and concat are supported. Shared results are copied at forks. Other nested MuData inputs and non-MuData returns are unsupported. Only public msmu functions can run. Environment differences are logged as warnings; packages are never installed or changed. The supplied object/log is not modified.

Returns:

Type Description MuData

A newly computed MuData with fresh history.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
# mdata must contain a supported file-backed workflow with recorded hashes.
reproduced = mm.pv.replay(mdata)

See get_log to inspect history, to_script for editable Python, and to_env for recorded package versions.

docs.title: msmu.pv.to_env
docs.text:
Export recorded Python/package versions for uv or conda, without installing.

format="uv" returns requirements.txt text; format="conda" returns environment.yml text with CPython/pip from conda-forge and Python packages in its pip section. With filename, write UTF-8 text (overwriting an existing file) and return None, as to_script does.

Accepts MuData or get_log() output, independently of replay support or hashes. By default, all referenced environments must agree on Python, package pins, platform and msmu source. Otherwise select a recorded environment_id. Numerical/thread settings may differ and are included as comments only.

These are version pins, not lockfiles: original package sources, conda builds, native dependencies and uncommitted code cannot be reconstructed. Only recorded CPython environments are supported. The supplied history is unchanged.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default history MuData | dict

MuData or decoded history from get_log.

required filename str | Path | None

Optional output file path; an existing file is overwritten.

None format str

"uv" for requirements.txt text or "conda" for environment.yml text.

'uv' environment_id str | None

Recorded environment ID to export. If omitted, all referenced environments must agree on the required version/source fields.

None

Returns:

Type Description str | None

Environment specification string when no filename is supplied; otherwise None.

Notes

Use get_log to find environment IDs. This does not install packages or mutate history.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
requirements = mm.pv.to_env(mdata, format="uv")

docs.title: msmu.pv.to_script
docs.text:
Generate editable Python calls with source/output hash checks.

If filename is supplied, write UTF-8 Python source (overwriting an existing file) and return None. Otherwise return the source text.

Accepts the same file-backed histories and options as replay(). The generated script requires msmu, checks the recorded environment at execution, and leaves its final MuData in mdata. Scripts enable hashing even when verification is disabled. Generation neither reads inputs nor executes calls.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default history MuData | dict

MuData or decoded history from get_log; supported workflows are described by replay.

required filename str | Path | None

Optional output path; an existing file is overwritten.

None sources dict | None

Mapping from recorded file paths/URLs to replacements, as in replay.

None verify bool

Include input/output hash verification. Requires recorded hashes when True and checks the current MuData against the last recorded output before export.

True

Returns:

Type Description str | None

Python source string when filename is omitted; otherwise None after writing the file.

Notes

Export does not execute the workflow or modify the supplied history. Decoded histories have no current MuData to compare. A failed validation leaves the destination file unchanged.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
script = mm.pv.to_script(mdata)

docs.title: msmu.tl.pca
docs.text:
Perform principal component analysis (PCA) on the specified modality of the MuData object.

This uses the scikit-learn implementation described by Pedregosa et al. (2011). For background on PCA, see Maćkiewicz and Ratajczak (1993).

  • Repository
  • Documentation

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData object containing the data.

required modality str

The modality to perform PCA on.

required layer str | None

Layer to use for quantification aggregation. If None, the default layer (.X) will be used. Defaults to "scaled".

None n_components int | None

Number of components to keep. if n_components is not set all components are kept::

n_components == min(n_samples, n_features)

If n_components == 'mle' and svd_solver == 'full', Minka's MLE is used to guess the dimension. Use of n_components == 'mle' will interpret svd_solver == 'auto' as svd_solver == 'full'.

If 0 < n_components < 1 and svd_solver == 'full', select the number of components such that the amount of variance that needs to be explained is greater than the percentage specified by n_components.

If svd_solver == 'arpack', the number of components must be strictly less than the minimum of n_features and n_samples.

Hence, the None case results in:

n_components == min(n_samples, n_features) - 1
None svd_solver Literal['auto', 'full', 'arpack', 'randomized']

"auto": The solver is selected by a default 'auto' policy is based on X.shape and n_components: if the input data has fewer than 1000 features and more than 10 times as many samples, then the "covariance_eigh" solver is used. Otherwise, if the input data is larger than 500x500 and the number of components to extract is lower than 80% of the smallest dimension of the data, then the more efficient "randomized" method is selected. Otherwise the exact "full" SVD is computed and optionally truncated afterward.

"full" : Run exact full SVD calling the standard LAPACK solver via scipy.linalg.svd and select the components by postprocessing

"arpack" : Run SVD truncated to n_components calling ARPACK solver via scipy.sparse.linalg.svds. It requires strictly 0 < n_components < min(X.shape)

"randomized" : Run randomized SVD by the method of Halko et al. (2011).

'auto' random_state int | None

Used when the 'arpack' or 'randomized' solvers are used. Pass an int for reproducible results across multiple function calls.

0 key_added str

Base key used for PCA outputs. Results are stored in: - .obsm[key_added] for component scores - .varm[key_added] for loadings - .uns[key_added] for explained variance metadata Defaults to "X_pca".

'X_pca' **kwargs Any

Additional keyword arguments passed to the PCA constructor.

{}

Returns:

Type Description MuData

Updated MuData object with PCA results.

References

Pedregosa, F. et al. Scikit-learn: machine learning in Python. Journal of Machine Learning Research 12, 2825–2830 (2011). Full text.

Maćkiewicz, A. and Ratajczak, W. Principal components analysis (PCA). Computers & Geosciences 19, 303–342 (1993). https://doi.org/10.1016/0098-3004(93)90090-r.

Halko, N., Martinsson, P. G., and Tropp, J. A. Finding structure with randomness: probabilistic algorithms for constructing approximate matrix decompositions. SIAM Review 53, 217–288 (2011). https://doi.org/10.1137/090771806.

docs.title: msmu.tl.run_de
docs.text:
Run Differential Expression Analysis (DEA) between two groups in a MuData object.

The analysis reads as four stages: (1) data validation — prepare the inputs once and let the engine mask the usable features; (2) test — the engine-specific statistic; (3) fold change — engine-independent group centers and the log2 fold change; (4) fold-change guidance line.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData object containing the data.

required modality str

Modality name within the MuData to analyze.

required category str

.obs column containing the group labels.

required ctrl str

Name of the control group.

required expr str | None

Name of the experimental group. If None, all other groups are used (not supported for stat_method="limma", which needs an explicit group).

None layer str | None

Layer containing intensities. If None, uses .X. Defaults to None.

None min_pct float

Minimum observed fraction required in every compared group or design cell. Defaults to 0.0; the selected test must still be estimable. Features below this threshold have NaN in p_value and q_value.

0.0 stat_method Literal['welch', 'student', 'wilcoxon', 'limma']

Statistical method: "limma" (moderated-t, default), or "welch", "student", or "wilcoxon" (label permutation).

'limma' n_resamples int

Number of label permutations; must be a positive integer for permutation methods. Defaults to 1000. Ignored by limma.

1000 log_transformed bool

Whether input is already log2-transformed. Defaults to True. Limma expects log2-transformed input.

True interaction str | None

limma only — .obs column of a second factor. If set, tests the interaction (difference-in-differences) of expr - ctrl across two of its levels.

None interaction_levels list | None

limma only — the two interaction levels to contrast.

None covariates list[str] | None

limma only — .obs columns to adjust for.

None p_adjust str

Correction for q_value: "auto", "bh", "by", "bonferroni", "holm", "hochberg", "hommel", or "empirical". Defaults to "auto": "bh" for limma and "empirical" for permutation methods. "empirical" is permutation-only.

'auto' _force_resample bool

If True, forces resampling even if the number of resamples exceeds the number of combinations.

False

Returns:

Type Description DeaResult

DeaResult containing DE analysis results.

Notes

The returned result provides .to_df() with features, repr_ctrl, repr_expr, pct_ctrl, pct_expr, log2fc, statistic, p_value, and q_value. .plot_volcano(...) delegates to plot_volcano, which uses raw p-values. The analysis returns a result object rather than a new MuData.

Examples:

import msmu as mm
result = mm.tl.run_de(mdata, modality="protein", category="condition", ctrl="control", expr="treated", stat_method="welch")
table = result.to_df()
fig = result.plot_volcano(log2fc_threshold=1.)

docs.title: msmu.tl.umap
docs.text:
Calculate UMAP embedding for a given modality in MuData object.

UMAP is described by McInnes et al. (2018).

  • Repository
  • Documentation

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default mdata MuData

MuData object containing the data.

required modality str

The modality to perform UMAP on.

required n_components int

The dimension of the space to embed into. This defaults to 2 to provide easy visualization, but can reasonably be set to any integer value in the range 2 to 100.

2 n_neighbors int | None

The size of local neighborhood (in terms of number of neighboring sample points) used for manifold approximation. Larger values result in more global views of the manifold, while smaller values result in more local data being preserved. In general values should be in the range 2 to 100.

15 layer str | None

Layer to use for quantification aggregation. If None, the default layer (.X) will be used. Defaults to None.

None metric str

The metric to use to compute distances in high dimensional space. If a string is passed it must match a valid predefined metric. If a general metric is required a function that takes two 1d arrays and returns a float can be provided. For performance purposes it is required that this be a numba jit'd function. Valid string metrics include:

  • euclidean
  • manhattan
  • chebyshev
  • minkowski
  • canberra
  • braycurtis
  • mahalanobis
  • wminkowski
  • seuclidean
  • cosine
  • correlation
  • haversine
  • hamming
  • jaccard
  • dice
  • russelrao
  • kulsinski
  • ll_dirichlet
  • hellinger
  • rogerstanimoto
  • sokalmichener
  • sokalsneath
  • yule

Metrics that take arguments (such as minkowski, mahalanobis etc.) can have arguments passed via the metric_kwds dictionary. At this time care must be taken and dictionary elements must be ordered appropriately; this will hopefully be fixed in the future.

'euclidean' init str

How to initialize the low dimensional embedding. Options are:

  • 'spectral': use a spectral embedding of the fuzzy 1-skeleton
  • 'random': assign initial embedding positions at random.
  • 'pca': use the first n_components from PCA applied to the input data.
  • 'tswspectral': use a spectral embedding of the fuzzy 1-skeleton, using a truncated singular value decomposition to "warm" up the eigensolver. This is intended as an alternative to the 'spectral' method, if that takes an excessively long time to complete initialization (or fails to complete).
  • A numpy array of initial embedding positions.
'random' min_dist float

The effective minimum distance between embedded points. Smaller values will result in a more clustered/clumped embedding where nearby points on the manifold are drawn closer together, while larger values will result on a more even dispersal of points. The value should be set relative to the spread value, which determines the scale at which embedded points will be spread out.

0.1 random_state int | None

RandomState instance or None, optional (default: None) If int, random_state is the seed used by the random number generator; If RandomState instance, random_state is the random number generator; If None, the random number generator is the RandomState instance used by np.random.

None key_added str

Base key used for UMAP outputs. Results are stored in: - .obsm[key_added] for embedding coordinates - .uns[key_added] for embedding metadata Defaults to "X_umap".

'X_umap' **kwargs Any

Additional keyword arguments passed to the UMAP constructor.

{}

Returns:

Type Description MuData

Updated MuData object with UMAP results.

References

McInnes, L., Healy, J., and Melville, J. UMAP: uniform manifold approximation and projection for dimension reduction. arXiv:1802.03426 (2018). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1802.03426.

docs.title: DDA - label-free¶
docs.text: This tutorial demonstrates how to analyze label-free quantification (LFQ) data from data-dependent acquisition (DDA) using the msmu package.

docs.title: Data preparation¶
docs.text:
The original dataset, described by Uszkoreit et al. (2022), is available as PXD012986. The search was performed with Sage v0.14.7 (Lazear (2023)).

For demonstration purposes, the example dataset was reduced to six samples and a total of 5,000 PSMs.

docs.title: Load required packages¶
docs.text: If you haven't installed the msmu package yet, please follow the installation guide.

docs.title: Read data¶
docs.text:
You can read data from various proteomics software outputs. Below are examples for Sage, MaxQuant, and FragPipe formats.

For this tutorial, we will use the Sage output as an example.

read_sage() function reads the Sage output files (lfq.tsv, results.sage.tsv) and creates modalities at MuData object.

docs.title: Saving raw MuData object¶
docs.text: After reading the search output, saving the MuData object as an h5mu file is recommended for future use.

docs.title: Filtering - PSM¶
docs.text:
You can filter the data based on the column values, such as q-value. You can also filter on the flags the reader records, such as contaminant, or on string containment.

Filtering is split into two steps: first, you mark a filter condition using mm.pp.add_filter(), and then you apply the filter using mm.pp.apply_filter().

Here, we keep protein groups with q-value < 0.01.

docs.title: Summarization - peptide¶
docs.text: You can summarize PSM-level data to peptide-level data using the mm.pp.to_peptide() function.

docs.title: Optional: Quantification with FlashLFQ¶
docs.text:
Peptide intensities can also be obtained with FlashLFQ (Millikin et al. (2018)). Export the filtered PSMs using mm.io.write_flashlfq_input(), then run FlashLFQ with the corresponding spectra. Attach the resulting QuantifiedPeptides.tsv using mm.io.add_quant(). This replaces the peptide intensity matrix while retaining the identification annotations. Continue with peptide filtering, normalization, and protein inference below.

The default workflow uses Sage intensities; uncomment the cell below to use FlashLFQ.

  1. Export the filtered PSMs.
  2. Run FlashLFQ with the corresponding spectra. Follow the official FlashLFQ instructions for installation and settings. For this example, you can skip the external run and use the provided result for the same six samples.
  3. Attach the peptide intensities from QuantifiedPeptides.tsv. Replace the example URL with your own result when running FlashLFQ on other data.

docs.title: Normalization¶
docs.text:
Here, we log2 transform and normalize the data at the peptide level.

Median centering normalization is applied using mm.pp.normalize() function.

docs.title: Protein inference¶
docs.text: You can infer protein-level data from peptide-level data using the mm.pp.infer_protein() function.

docs.title: Summarization - protein¶
docs.text:
You can summarize peptide-level data to protein-level data using the mm.pp.to_protein() function.

By default, all peptides within a protein group are used for protein group quantification aggregation. Set top_n (e.g., 3) to use only the top-ranked peptides.

docs.title: Saving processed MuData object¶
docs.text: You can save MuData object into an h5mu file. This allows you to easily reload the processed data in future sessions without repeating the entire analysis pipeline.

docs.title: References¶
docs.text:
Uszkoreit, J., Barkovits, K., Pacharra, S., Pfeiffer, K., Steinbach, S., Marcus, K., and Eisenacher, M. Dataset containing physiological amounts of spike-in proteins into murine C2C12 background as a ground truth quantitative LC-MS/MS reference. Data in Brief 43, 108435 (2022).

Lazear, M. R. Sage: an open-source tool for fast proteomics searching and quantification at scale. Journal of Proteome Research 22(11), 3652–3659 (2023).

Millikin, R. J., Solntsev, S. K., Shortreed, M. R., and Smith, L. M. Ultrafast peptide label-free quantification with FlashLFQ. Journal of Proteome Research 17(1), 386–391 (2018). https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jproteome.7b00608.

docs.title: DDA - TMT¶
docs.text: This tutorial demonstrates how to analyze tandem mass tag (TMT) labeled data from data-dependent acquisition (DDA) using msmu package.

docs.title: Data preparation¶
docs.text:
The original dataset, described by Magnusson et al. (2019), is available as PXD013361. The search was performed with Sage v0.14.7 (Lazear (2023)).

For demonstration purposes, the example dataset has been trimmed to include only 5,000 PSMs.

docs.title: Load required packages¶
docs.text: If you haven't installed the msmu package yet, please follow the installation guide.

docs.title: Read data¶
docs.text:
You can read data from various proteomics software outputs. Below are examples for Sage, MaxQuant, and FragPipe formats.

For this tutorial, we will use the Sage output as an example.

read_sage() function reads the Sage output files (tmt.tsv, results.sage.tsv) and creates modalities at MuData object.

docs.title: Removing blank channels¶
docs.text: If your TMT data contains blank channels, you can remove them by subsetting MuData object.

docs.title: Saving raw MuData object¶
docs.text: After reading the search output, saving the MuData object as an h5mu file is recommended for future use.

docs.title: Filtering - PSM¶
docs.text:
You can filter the data based on the column values, such as q-value. You can also filter on the flags the reader records, such as contaminant, or on string containment.

Filtering is split into two steps: first, you mark a filter condition using mm.pp.add_filter(), and then you apply the filter using mm.pp.apply_filter().

Here, we keep protein groups with q-value < 0.01.

docs.title: Normalization¶
docs.text:
Here, we log2 transform and normalize the data at the PSM level.

Median centering normalization is applied using mm.pp.normalize() function.

Optionally, if you need to correct batch effects using global internal standard (GIS) channels, you can scale the data using mm.pp.correct_batch_effect() function. Make sure to have GIS channels in each TMT batch. The example code below assumes that the GIS channels are named with prefix POOLED_.

docs.title: Computing precursor isolation purity¶
docs.text:
For TMT data, it is recommended to compute precursor isolation purity to exclude low-purity features from quantification aggregation. compute_precursor_isolation_purity() function calculates precursor isolation purity using mzML files.

For demonstration purposes, we will skip this step in the tutorial.

docs.title: Summarization - peptide¶
docs.text:
You can summarize PSM-level data to peptide-level data using the mm.pp.to_peptide() function.

If isolation purity was calculated and purity_threshold parameter is set, features below this cutoff are excluded from quantification aggregation.

docs.title: Protein inference¶
docs.text: You can infer protein-level data from peptide-level data using the mm.pp.infer_protein() function.

docs.title: Summarization - protein¶
docs.text:
You can summarize peptide-level data to protein-level data using the mm.pp.to_protein() function.

As default, top 3 peptides within protein group can be used for protein group quantification aggregation. If top_n is None, all peptides will be used.

docs.title: Saving processed MuData object¶
docs.text: You can save MuData object into an h5mu file. This allows you to easily reload the processed data in future sessions without repeating the entire analysis pipeline.

docs.title: References¶
docs.text:
Magnusson, R. et al. A validated strategy to infer protein biomarkers from RNA-Seq by combining multiple mRNA splice variants and time-delay. bioRxiv 599373 (2019).

Lazear, M. R. Sage: an open-source tool for fast proteomics searching and quantification at scale. Journal of Proteome Research 22(11), 3652–3659 (2023).

docs.title: Differential expression (DE) analysis¶
docs.text:
Compare protein abundances between G1 and G2 using the processed DDA-LFQ dataset, inspect the results, and create volcano plots.

For method selection and interpretation, see How it works: DE analysis.

docs.title: Load processed data¶
docs.text: Complete DDA-LFQ with the current msmu version, then run this notebook from the same working directory. Load its processed dda_lfq_PXD012986.h5mu result, which already contains filtered, log2-transformed, and normalized protein data. G1 and G2 each contain three samples.

docs.title: Compare the two groups¶
docs.text:
Use mm.tl.run_de() to compare G2 (expr) against G1 (ctrl), using the factor value[condition] column in the protein modality's .obs. This call uses the default limma method and Benjamini–Hochberg correction (p_adjust="auto").

Set min_pct=0.5 to require observations in at least two of the three samples in each group. The input is already log2-transformed, so keep the default log_transformed=True; this argument describes the input and does not transform it. See the run_de() API reference for all parameters.

docs.title: Inspect DE results¶
docs.text:
Use DeaResult.to_df() to obtain a pandas DataFrame. Preview the feature identifiers, fold changes, p-values, and q-values below. For this comparison, a positive log2fc means higher abundance in G2. Use q_value for significance decisions across the tested proteins; p_value is unadjusted.

pct_ctrl and pct_expr show the percentages of observed samples in each group. Features without a usable test result have NaN in p_value and q_value.

docs.title: Visualize the comparison¶
docs.text: The volcano plot shows log2fc against -log10(p_value), using the raw p-value cutoff 0.05 and the fc_pct_5 fold-change threshold by default. Read q_value from the result table for multiple-testing significance.

docs.title: Optional: Run a permutation test¶
docs.text:
To use label permutation, set stat_method="welch" and request the number of label shuffles with n_resamples. This call uses empirical FDR correction by default; another correction can be selected with p_adjust.

Only 20 distinct three-versus-three label splits are available, so this call enumerates all of them. Increasing n_resamples cannot add new splits. The reported q-values depend on the data and correction method; treat the small-sample warning below as a design-level diagnostic rather than a universal q-value bound. See How it works: DE analysis for method details.

docs.title: DIA - label-free¶
docs.text: This tutorial demonstrates how to analyze label-free quantification (LFQ) data from data-independent acquisition (DIA) using the msmu package.

docs.title: Data preparation¶
docs.text:
The original dataset, described by Uszkoreit et al. (2022), is available as PXD012988. The search was performed with DIA-NN v2.1.0 (Demichev et al. (2020)).

For demonstration purposes, the example dataset was reduced to six samples and a total of 1,000 peptides.

docs.title: Load required packages¶
docs.text: If you haven't installed the msmu package yet, please follow the installation guide.

docs.title: Read data¶
docs.text:
You can read data from various proteomics software outputs. Below are examples for DIA-NN, MaxQuant, and FragPipe formats.

For this tutorial, we will use DIA-NN output as an example.

read_diann() function reads DIA-NN output file (report.parquet or report.tsv) and creates modalities at MuData object.

docs.title: Saving raw MuData object¶
docs.text: After reading the search output, saving the MuData object as an h5mu file is recommended for future use.

docs.title: Handling PSM level¶
docs.text: If you are using DIA-NN version under 2.0, or the data doesn't contain decoy features, please jump to this section.

docs.title: Filtering - PSM¶
docs.text:
You can filter the data based on the column values, such as q-value. You can also filter on the flags the reader records, such as contaminant, or on string containment.

Filtering is split into two steps: first, you mark a filter condition using mm.pp.add_filter(), and then you apply the filter using mm.pp.apply_filter().

Here, we keep protein groups with q-value < 0.01.

docs.title: Normalization¶
docs.text:
Here, we log2 transform and normalize the data at the PSM level.

Median centering normalization is applied using mm.pp.normalize() function.

docs.title: Summarization - peptide¶
docs.text: You can summarize PSM-level data to peptide-level data using the mm.pp.to_peptide() function.

docs.title: Protein inference¶
docs.text: You can infer protein-level data from peptide-level data using the mm.pp.infer_protein() function.

docs.title: Summarization - protein¶
docs.text:
You can summarize peptide-level data to protein-level data using the mm.pp.to_protein() function.

As default, top 3 peptides within protein group can be used for protein group quantification aggregation. If top_n is None, all peptides will be used.

docs.title: Saving processed MuData object¶
docs.text: You can save MuData object into an h5mu file. This allows you to easily reload the processed data in future sessions without repeating the entire analysis pipeline.

docs.title: For DIA-NN without decoy¶
docs.text:
DIA-NN versions earlier than 2.0 do not include decoy features in the final report.tsv.

Also, even in DIA-NN version higher than 2.0, if the search settings in DIA-NN does not contain --report-decoys, the final will still lack decoy features.

As a result, step-wise q-value estimation cannot be performed and mm.pp.infer_protein() cannot be applied to DIA-NN version under 2.0.

Therefore, the protein groups reported directly by DIA-NN should be used without re-inferring them in msmu.

docs.title: Filtering - without decoy¶
docs.text: For protein group–level q-values, use Lib.PG.Q.Value (when MBR is enabled) or Global.PG.Q.Value (when MBR is disabled) from the DIA-NN search results.

docs.title: Normalization - without decoy¶
docs.text: Once filtering is done, you can process and summarize the data to peptide and protein levels as shown below.

docs.title: Summarization - without decoy¶
docs.text:
Manually add protein group and peptide-type information from the DIA-NN search results into the peptide .var:

  • protein_group from DIA-NN's Protein.Group (string value representing the protein group IDs associated with the peptide)
  • peptide_type from DIA-NN's Proteotypic (boolean value indicating whether the peptide is unique to a single protein group or shared among multiple protein groups).

No peptide filtering is performed at this stage.

docs.title: References¶
docs.text:
Uszkoreit, J., Barkovits, K., Pacharra, S., Pfeiffer, K., Steinbach, S., Marcus, K., and Eisenacher, M. Dataset containing physiological amounts of spike-in proteins into murine C2C12 background as a ground truth quantitative LC-MS/MS reference. Data in Brief 43, 108435 (2022).

Demichev, V., Messner, C. B., Vernardis, S. I., Lilley, K. S., and Ralser, M. DIA-NN: neural networks and interference correction enable deep proteome coverage in high throughput. Nature Methods 17(1), 41–44 (2020).

docs.title: Post-translational modification (PTM)¶
docs.text: This tutorial shows how to process and analyze PTM data using msmu. We will use a mock oxidation-site dataset for demonstration.

docs.title: Load a recorded result¶
docs.text: Complete DDA-TMT with the current msmu version, then run this notebook from the same working directory. Its processed result, dda_tmt_PXD013361.h5mu, contains peptide and protein modalities on a log2 scale.

docs.title: Reuse global protein data¶
docs.text: For this demonstration, use the processed protein modality from the same DDA-TMT result as the global protein reference. In a real PTM experiment, process the matching global protein dataset separately and use that result for adjustment.

docs.title: PTM site summarization¶
docs.text:
PTM sites are localized from each peptide's own protein accessions and the attached FASTA, so no protein inference is needed on the PTM side. Site IDs therefore depend only on the peptide and the FASTA -- the same PTM data yields the same sites whether or not a global dataset is involved.

We need the FASTA file that contains the protein sequences used for site localization.

docs.title: PTM quantification adjustment by global protein levels¶
docs.text:
mm.pp.adjust_ptm_by_protein() computes differential PTM usage: each site's log intensity minus its parent protein's, so a site's change reads relative to whatever its protein did.

A site's denominator is found through the accessions it was localized on, translated into a global protein group via the global dataset's protein_map. Nothing is looked up by peptide, so a PTM peptide the global run never observed is still adjustable whenever its protein was quantified there -- the common case under enrichment.

The adjusted values replace the quantification that was read, as with every other msmu transform. Sites that could not be adjusted become NaN, and .var["adjustment_status"] records why for each one. Use mm.dt.save_layer() first if you want to keep the unadjusted values alongside.

docs.title: 2024 Fulcher et al. tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial analyzes paired single-cell RNA and proteomics data from C10 and SVEC cells in Fulcher et al. (2024). msmu processes Sage identifications and FlashLFQ peptide intensities and records the proteomics preprocessing steps. scanpy, PIMMS, muon, and MOFA provide RNA processing, protein imputation, and multi-omics analysis.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
Use docs/tutorials/2024_Fulcher as the working directory. For the main analysis, run 01 → 02 for proteins and 03 for RNA, then combine their outputs in 04. The protein and RNA notebooks download their inputs. Appendix A (workflow export and verification) and Appendix B (publication figures) are optional and can be skipped when following the main analysis.

Notebook Purpose Main outputs 01 Process proteomics data Filter identifications, normalize peptides, and summarize proteins MSV000089280.h5mu 02 Impute protein data Fill missing protein intensities with PIMMS MSV000089280_imputed.h5mu 03 Process scRNA-seq data Map RNA counts to SDRF cell IDs, filter genes, and normalize GSE201575.h5ad 04 Integrate multi-omics data Combine paired modalities, compute WNN UMAP, and fit MOFA Fulcher_multimodal.h5mu, MOFA_model.hdf5 Appendix A: Export and verify Export the recorded workflow and compare protein-processing checkpoints requirements.txt, script.py Appendix B: Generate publication figures Calculate differential expression and checkpoint comparisons, style figure panels, and export SVGs Figures

MSV000089280.h5mu is the processed checkpoint before imputation, with log₂-transformed, normalized, and summarized protein intensities. MSV000089280_imputed.h5mu also contains the PIMMS imputed layer used for WNN. Differential expression and MOFA use the observed protein matrix.

The verification section in Appendix A and the comparison figures in Appendix B require a separately prepared MSV000089280_debian.h5mu described in Appendix A. Appendix A compares the two checkpoints and fits both differential-expression analyses in the current Python session.

docs.title: Environment setup
docs.text: The recorded preprocessing environment uses Python 3.13.5 and msmu 0.4.3. Download requirements.txt for the exported package versions, including scanpy, PIMMS, muon, and MOFA dependencies.

docs.title: References
docs.text: Fulcher, J. M. et al. Parallel measurement of transcriptomes and proteomes from same single cells using nanodroplet splitting. Nature Communications 15, 10614 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-54099-z.

docs.title: Export requirements and a script with verification¶
docs.text:
mm.pv.to_env() writes the recorded Python package requirements to requirements.txt. mm.pv.to_script(..., verify=True) writes script.py with checks for the environment, recorded inputs, and output hashes when the script is run.

Exporting these files does not execute the workflow or establish successful replay. Run the generated script separately with its referenced upstream inputs available. The requirements capture version pins, but do not restore native libraries, thread settings, or uncommitted source edits.

docs.title: Recreate the environment and run the script (e.g., on Debian)¶
docs.text:
On Debian, run from the directory containing requirements.txt, script.py, and the original MSV000089280/ input folder. Create the recorded environment with uv, append the checkpoint save to script.py, and run it:

uv venv --python 3.13.5 .venv-replay
uv pip sync --python .venv-replay/bin/python requirements.txt
printf '\nmdata.write_h5mu("MSV000089280_debian.h5mu")\n' >> script.py
uv run --no-project --python .venv-replay/bin/python python script.py

After successful completion, copy MSV000089280_debian.h5mu to this tutorial directory on macOS for the comparison below.

def fetch_protein_label(accession):
    response = requests.get(
        f"https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/{accession}.json",
        params={"fields": "gene_primary"},
        timeout=30,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    for gene in response.json().get("genes", []):
        name = gene.get("geneName", {}).get("value")
        if name:
            return name.upper()
    return accession
